327.history: The small mill town on the north coast stands beside Taigh-solais Muileann bheag, the only one of the five lights to burn coal. Its keeper Ailig mac Griogair asked three winters running to go back to the old lamp, and its fishermen complained that the colour the coal flame cast on the water drove the herring off. Lowe came to see the flame and the keeper's son answered him on the point. Within a season the herring came back, and the complaint was withdrawn. In the stoppage of the hundred and forty-third year its pits stopped with the rest. The coal flame's colour on the water was still remarked by every stranger who passed the cape at night.

135.history: The large farming village in the deep fields above the workings became a camp when the new galleries were opened into its hill, and it was the worst place on the hill in the spotted pox. Beitris Bhàn laid out its dead at her own table, the washing-women first said there that the girl of the spoil-houses did not grow, and Anne Colby kept her sick-house of canvas there through the Green Death, which began among its huts. Walter Crane walked its sick-rows. Its granaries fed the camps for a century. The feather Beitris Bhàn nailed over her own door was copied on doors across the camps as fast as the overseers pulled them down, and the roll of the camp keeps the first cases of the Green Death under her name.
135.known_for: the camp where the Green Death began

461.history: The temple village of Macha at the edge of the workings kept a small shrine where the pit crews left the first piece of coal from every new gallery. The Company suffered the custom, since it cost a stone a gallery, and the shrine was one of the two pit-mouth shrines where the crews kept the old words of the rock face in the strangers' years. It lies beside Ceann leathan, where the old contest is still held each year, and its druids tended the shrine through the whole of the age without a Company quarrel.

393.history: The grey ford beside Cathair mhòr is remembered for Sìne Ruadh, custodian in the Green Death, who ordered every hut where a death had been burned with its bedding. The Company protested the loss of its property, and the custodians noted that the sickness stopped sooner at Àth ghlas than anywhere else. The story was still told by grandparents in the fever years sixty years later. It lies a short way from the ruin of Làrach an Dùin-fhaire, which is older than any dwelling of the Dia-thìrich, and the huts it burned were never rebuilt on the same ground.

318.history: The holy hill south of the capital laid the dead of the Green Death in its shrine's burial ground until it was full, and then in the field beside it, which was never ploughed again. In the months before the rising the crew-leaders of the north met by night on the moor above it and raised a cairn of spoil-stones from their own pits; the nineteen dead of the ford at Àth chiar were buried within sight of it. It has been a house of Macha since An Aois Scaraidh, and lies close by the old battlefield of Muileann ghlas.
318.known_for: the unploughed field and the two cairns

366.history: The harbour of the calm strait was chosen by Tolley in his first month as Commissioner for a quarantine station, holding every ship from an Tìr Thall offshore until a physician had looked her crew over. It was the first order of his rule the Dia-thìrich approved, and they said so. Its quays stand on Eilean chrom across the strait, and the physician's boat went out from them to every ship that came in under the quarantine.
